idiom_name: interface wrapper delegating to the adaptee (object adapter), plus an optional factory
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare the interface the client wants (Target), leave the incompatible component untouched (Adaptee), and add one adapter whose members implement Target by translating each call into one or more adaptee calls. Prefer the object form - the adapter holds or borrows an adaptee instance, so it works with subclasses, sealed/final types and dependency injection - and reserve the inheritance-based class adapter for languages that split interface inheritance from implementation inheritance and for the rare case where the adaptee's protected members or overridable behaviour are needed. Keep the adapter a translation layer: map names, parameter order, argument shapes, units, null/optionality and errors, and document every semantic change. Where several adaptees must be selectable, add a small factory or registry that picks the adapter for a configured provider. If Target needs a single operation, a function or closure capturing the adaptee is the same pattern at function granularity.
pitfalls: Exposing the adaptee's own interface through the adapter re-couples the client and undoes the pattern.
Translation that only renames members while ignoring semantics (units, errors, null handling) yields plausible-looking wrong results.
One adapter per adaptee: a shared 'god adapter' accumulating provider-specific logic becomes the coupling it was meant to remove.
Sharing mutable adaptee state between clients without deciding who owns and closes it.
Silently emulating a capability the adaptee lacks: returning plausible defaults or swallowing NotImplementedError masks real gaps and produces wrong results that only surface in production.

Sync-to-async or async-to-sync bridging without explicit timeout and cancellation handling can cause deadlocks; always isolate synchronous libraries behind an adapter that enforces a timeout boundary.

In dynamic or duck-typed languages, an adapter that drifts out of sync with the target interface produces wrong results at runtime with no compiler signal; use structural type checking or contract tests to catch drift.
Performance overhead in high-frequency or hot-path code: one delegation hop per call is negligible at a boundary but measurable inside tight loops or microsecond-sensitive paths.

Two-way adapters that try to serve both translation directions simultaneously confuse callers about which interface is authoritative; prefer unidirectional adapters and explicit reverse translation when needed.
Inadvertent state coupling: multiple adapter instances sharing a mutable adaptee reference without synchronisation produces subtle cross-request contamination.
Map an unknown vendor error to success or a generic default -> callers make retry or commit decisions on false information -> preserve the target error taxonomy and fail closed on unmapped cases.

Buffer an unbounded stream to imitate a batch-shaped target -> latency and memory grow with input size and backpressure disappears -> preserve streaming semantics or define an explicit bounded conversion.
Put provider selection inside adapter methods -> configuration branches duplicate translation paths and drift -> select one adapter at composition time and keep each adapter's mapping deterministic.
